questions.text: What command do you run to create a new Next.js project?
questions.explanation: The official way to scaffold a new Next.js project is by running `npx create-next-app@latest`. This command sets up the project structure, installs dependencies, and optionally configures TypeScript, Tailwind, and the App Router. It is the recommended starting point from the Next.js documentation.

questions.text: Which file is the entry point for global styles in a Next.js project?
questions.explanation: In a Next.js project, `globals.css` is the file where you define styles that apply across every page. It is imported in `_app.js` (Pages Router) or the root `layout.js` (App Router). Styles defined here are available throughout the entire application.

questions.text: What is the default port Next.js runs on in development?
questions.explanation: When you run `npm run dev`, Next.js starts a local development server on port 3000 by default. You can access your app at `http://localhost:3000`. The port can be changed by passing a `-p` flag to the dev command.

questions.text: In the Pages Router, what file would you create to handle the `/contact` route?
questions.explanation: Next.js uses file-based routing in the Pages Router, meaning the file path inside the `pages` directory maps directly to the URL. To create a `/contact` route, you create `pages/contact.js`. Next.js automatically registers it as a route without any additional configuration.

questions.text: Which Next.js component optimizes images automatically?
questions.explanation: Next.js provides the `<Image>` component from `next/image` which automatically optimizes images by resizing, compressing, and serving them in modern formats like WebP. It also handles lazy loading by default, improving page performance without manual configuration.

questions.text: What does `npm run build` do in a Next.js project?
questions.explanation: `npm run build` compiles and optimizes your Next.js application for production. It pre-renders static pages, bundles JavaScript, and outputs the result to the `.next` folder. This build output is what gets deployed to a production server.

answerOptions.text: Runs unit tests for the project
Compiles and optimizes the app for production

questions.text: How do you create a dynamic route for a blog post in the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: In the Pages Router, dynamic route segments are defined using square bracket notation in the filename. A file named `pages/posts/[id].js` matches any route like `/posts/1` or `/posts/hello`. The dynamic segment is accessible via `useRouter` or `getStaticProps`.

questions.text: Which hook do you use to access the current route information in a Next.js Pages Router component?
questions.explanation: `useRouter` from `next/router` gives you access to the current route object, including the pathname, query parameters, and dynamic segments. It is the standard way to read routing information inside a component in the Pages Router.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the `public` folder in a Next.js project?
questions.explanation: The `public` folder is used to serve static assets like images, fonts, and icons directly. Files placed in this folder are accessible at the root URL — for example, `public/logo.png` is available at `/logo.png`. Next.js serves these files without any processing.

answerOptions.text: It serves static assets directly at the root URL

questions.text: In Next.js, where do you create API routes when using the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: API routes in the Pages Router are created by adding files inside the `pages/api` directory. Each file exports a default function that handles HTTP requests and responses. For example, `pages/api/hello.js` becomes accessible at `/api/hello`.

questions.text: What is the file convention for the App Router's root layout?
questions.explanation: In the App Router, the root layout is defined in `app/layout.js`. This file wraps every page in the application and must include the `<html>` and `<body>` tags. It is required and cannot be removed from an App Router project.

questions.text: How do you add environment variables in Next.js that are accessible on the server only?
questions.explanation: Environment variables defined in a `.env.local` file without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix are only available server-side. Next.js automatically loads this file and keeps those variables out of the client bundle. This is important for secrets like API keys that should never be exposed to the browser.

answerOptions.text: Store them in .env.local without any prefix
Add them to next.config.js under the env key
Store them in a secrets.js file in the root

questions.text: What prefix must an environment variable have to be accessible in the browser in Next.js?
questions.explanation: Next.js only exposes environment variables to the client-side bundle if they are prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. Without this prefix, the variable remains server-side only. This design prevents accidental exposure of sensitive values to the browser.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes Next.js?
questions.explanation: Next.js is a React framework that adds server-side rendering, static site generation, file-based routing, and API routes on top of React. It is not a standalone language or a replacement for React — it builds on React to provide production-ready features out of the box.

answerOptions.text: A CSS framework for styling React applications
A React framework that adds SSR, routing, and other production features
A replacement for React with its own component model
A database ORM for Node.js applications
A testing library for React components

questions.text: What does the `_app.js` file do in the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: `_app.js` is a special file in the Pages Router that wraps every page component. It is used to persist layouts, global state, or global styles across page navigations. Any component or provider placed in `_app.js` remains mounted as the user navigates between pages.

answerOptions.text: It defines the home page of the application
It wraps every page and is used for global layouts and providers
It configures the Next.js build pipeline

questions.text: How do you navigate programmatically to another page in the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: The `useRouter` hook provides a `push` method that navigates to a new route programmatically. Calling `router.push('/about')` works like clicking a `<Link>` component but from within a function, such as after a form submission or button click.

questions.text: What is the purpose of `next.config.js`?
questions.explanation: `next.config.js` is the configuration file for a Next.js project. It lets you customize build behavior, set environment variables, configure redirects and rewrites, and enable experimental features. It is loaded by Next.js at build time and is not bundled into the client.

answerOptions.text: It defines the database connection for the app
It customizes Next.js build and runtime behavior
It sets up React context providers
It replaces package.json for dependency management

questions.text: In the App Router, what file do you create to define a page at a given route?
questions.explanation: In the App Router, a `page.js` file inside a folder defines the UI for that route. For example, `app/about/page.js` renders the `/about` page. Without a `page.js` file, the folder is not treated as a publicly accessible route even if it contains other files like layouts.

questions.text: What does CSS Modules provide in a Next.js project?
questions.explanation: CSS Modules scope styles locally to the component that imports them, preventing class name conflicts across the application. In Next.js, any file ending in `.module.css` is treated as a CSS Module. Class names are automatically transformed to unique identifiers at build time.

answerOptions.text: A way to write CSS in JavaScript using template literals
Global styles that apply to every component
Locally scoped styles that prevent class name conflicts
A built-in alternative to Tailwind CSS
Server-side style injection for SSR pages

questions.text: What is the difference between `npm run dev` and `npm run start` in Next.js?
questions.explanation: `npm run dev` starts the development server with hot reloading and detailed error messages intended for development. `npm run start` serves the production build created by `npm run build` and should only be used after building the app. Running `start` without a prior build will fail.

answerOptions.text: There is no difference; both start the same server
`dev` runs the development server; `start` serves the production build
`start` runs the development server; `dev` serves the production build

questions.text: How do you pass data between a parent and child component in Next.js?
questions.explanation: Next.js uses React's component model, so data is passed from parent to child via props. The parent component includes the child in its JSX and passes values as attributes, which the child receives as a props object. This is standard React behavior and is not specific to Next.js.

answerOptions.text: Using the Next.js context API built into the framework
Via props, the same as standard React
Through a global store that Next.js manages automatically

questions.text: What is pre-rendering in Next.js?
questions.explanation: Pre-rendering means Next.js generates the HTML for a page in advance rather than having the browser build it entirely from JavaScript. This improves initial load performance and makes pages more accessible to search engine crawlers. Next.js pre-renders every page by default using either static generation or server-side rendering.

answerOptions.text: Compiling TypeScript to JavaScript before the build
Generating HTML for pages in advance rather than fully in the browser
Caching API responses before they are requested
Loading images before the rest of the page content
Running middleware before a page renders on the client

questions.text: What is the purpose of the `<Head>` component from `next/head` in the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: The `<Head>` component lets you add elements to the HTML `<head>` tag from within any page or component, such as `<title>`, `<meta>`, and `<link>` tags. This is how you set page titles and SEO metadata on a per-page basis in the Pages Router. In the App Router this is handled differently using the metadata API.

answerOptions.text: It renders the header navigation bar at the top of the page
It injects elements like title and meta tags into the HTML head
It defines the root layout shared across all pages
It pre-fetches linked pages for faster navigation

questions.text: What happens when you add a file called `404.js` inside the `pages` directory?
questions.explanation: Placing a `404.js` file in the `pages` directory creates a custom 404 error page that Next.js serves whenever a route is not found. Without this file, Next.js displays its default 404 page. This lets you style the error page to match the rest of your application.

answerOptions.text: It creates a route accessible at /404
It defines a custom page shown when a route is not found
It logs 404 errors to the console during development

questions.text: Which of the following is true about static generation in Next.js?
questions.explanation: Static generation produces HTML at build time, meaning the page is generated once and reused on every request. This makes it the fastest rendering method since no server computation is needed per request. It is best suited for pages where the content does not change frequently, such as marketing pages or blog posts.

answerOptions.text: HTML is generated on the server for every incoming request
HTML is generated at build time and reused on every request
HTML is generated entirely in the browser using JavaScript
HTML is generated only after the user logs in
HTML is generated by the CDN based on user location
